summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Visitors in Nouvelle-Aquitaine stand under the national framework: French law on identity documents, anti-discrimination, marriage and criminal law applies uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions. No division-specific transgender findings appear in the surviving sources; the national mechanisms they document apply here unchanged.

Prison placement follows the sex inscribed on identity documents. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so trans women whose legal gender is marked male, the vast majority without sex-reassignment surgery, are placed in men's facilities. A detainee recalled inmates shouting "We don't want any women here!" and threats of violence.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

One of the five establishments inspected for the CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021, the prison at Saint-Martin-de-Ré in Charente-Maritime, lies within Nouvelle-Aquitaine. The opinion records no separate finding against that establishment; its conclusions are stated for adult prisons as a class.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 records the persistence of serious violations of trans detainees' fundamental rights in adult prisons, while noting that none were observed in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The distinction matters for a visitor weighing where custody risk actually sits.

That review covered the situations of some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station. It is a follow-up to the CGLPL opinion of 30 June 2010.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.
localsOnly:
Prison placement is decided facility by facility rather than by statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held follows the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each establishment improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison; the BuzzFeed News feature illustrates this with the case of American trans woman Kara B., held in conditions Hazan describes as worrying.

The CGLPL examined roughly forty referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued its opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

The Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights sets out official guidance for service providers alongside its finding of persistent violations.
outOfScopeNotes:
No division-specific enforcement data for Nouvelle-Aquitaine appears in the surviving sources. Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented in establishments within this region is unresolved and not sourced here.

The CGLPL opinion names Saint-Martin-de-Ré among the prisons inspected but records no separate outcome or finding for that establishment; its conclusions are stated collectively for adult prisons.

The border account is a single first-person narrative published on 7 March 2017. No statistics on identity-document checks at entry points serving this region are available in the inventory, and the frequency of such checks is unresolved.

No information is sourced on identity-document issuance or amendment practice for trans residents of this region, including turnaround times or grounds for refusal.

Louna's placement remains before the French National Assembly under oral question no. 219; the outcome of that scrutiny is unresolved.
